posts.caption:
Inflation, explained simply 👇

Inflation means prices rise over time, so the same money buys less. It's why your coffee costs more than it used to.

Save this for the next time someone throws finance jargon at you. 🔖

New term every day. Follow @equivisionbasics.

Educational content only, not financial advice.

#inflation #prices #finance #personalfinance #financialliteracy #moneybasics #learnfinance

slides.headline: Inflation means [[prices rise]] over time, so your money [[buys less]].
Your morning coffee costs [[$4.00]]. A year later, it costs $4.20.

steps.title: That 5% rise is the inflation rate

slides.label: THE EFFECT
slides.headline: Same money, less stuff.
slides.sub: When prices rise, each dollar [[buys less]] than before.
slides.note: Example uses 5% inflation. Real rates vary by country and year.

slides.headline: Why it [[matters]] to you.
slides.sub: If your pay or savings don't keep up, you can afford less.

rows.text: Cash sitting still **slowly loses buying power**
Pay and savings that **grow faster than prices** keep up

slides.note: Many central banks aim for about 2% inflation a year.

slides.title: Inflation = Rising prices
slides.sub: Your money didn't shrink. Prices grew.
checks: Aim to [[grow money faster]] than prices

posts.caption:
Stocks, explained simply 👇

A stock is a tiny slice of a company that you can own. If the company does well, your slice can grow in value. If not, it can fall.

Save this for the next time someone throws finance jargon at you. 🔖

New term every day. Follow @equivisionbasics.

Educational content only, not financial advice.

#stocks #investing #finance #personalfinance #financialliteracy #moneybasics #learnfinance

slides.headline: A stock is a [[tiny slice]] of a company that you can own.
slides.footer: Own a slice, share in the [[ups and downs]].

slides.headline: Imagine a pizza shop worth [[$1,000]], split into 100 slices.

steps.title: The shop is split into 100 shares
steps.sub: Each share is 1% of the business.

steps.title: Shop does well? Price rises
steps.sub: Your share might be worth $12 later.

slides.closing: You own a piece of the shop. That's a [[stock]].

slides.label: THE UPS AND DOWNS
slides.headline: Prices move both ways.
slides.sub: A share's price can [[rise or fall]] with the company and the market.
slides.note: It could also fall below $10. Stock prices are never guaranteed.

slides.headline: Why people [[buy stocks]].
slides.sub: Over long periods stocks have often grown, but the past isn't a promise.

rows.text: Company grows: the **share can rise** in value

slides.note: You can lose money. Never invest what you can't afford to lose.

slides.title: Stock = Ownership
slides.sub: You own a small piece of a company.
checks: A stock is **one slice** of a company
It's **never guaranteed**: you can lose money

posts.caption:
Dividend, explained simply 👇

A dividend is a cash payment a company shares with the people who own its stock. Think of it as a slice of the profit, paid out.

Save this for the next time someone throws finance jargon at you. 🔖

New term every day. Follow @equivisionbasics.

Educational content only, not financial advice.

#dividends #stocks #finance #personalfinance #financialliteracy #moneybasics #learnfinance

slides.headline: A dividend is a [[cash payment]] a company shares with its owners.

steps.title: The company earns a profit
steps.sub: It decides to share some of it.

steps.title: You receive $50 in cash
steps.sub: Often paid a few times a year.

slides.label: HOW IT ADDS UP
slides.headline: Small payments add up.
slides.sub: Dividends are usually paid [[a few times a year]].
slides.note: Illustrative example. Companies can raise, cut or skip dividends.

slides.headline: Dividends aren't [[guaranteed]].
slides.sub: A company chooses whether to pay one, and how much.

rows.text: A company can **cut or skip** its dividend

slides.note: Not every company pays one. Many growing companies reinvest instead.

slides.title: Dividend = Payout
slides.sub: A slice of profit paid to shareholders.
checks: Usually **cash, a few times a year**

posts.caption:
ETF, explained simply 👇

An ETF (Exchange-Traded Fund) is a basket of many investments that you can buy in one go, just like a single share.

Save this for the next time someone throws finance jargon at you. 🔖

New term every day. Follow @equivisionbasics.

Educational content only, not financial advice.

#etf #investing #finance #personalfinance #financialliteracy #moneybasics #learnfinance

slides.headline: An ETF is a [[basket]] of many investments you buy in one go.
Instead of picking [[100 stocks]] one by one...

steps.title: A fund company builds a basket
steps.sub: It holds lots of different stocks.

steps.title: You buy one share of the ETF
steps.sub: That one purchase covers the basket.

steps.title: It trades like a normal share
steps.sub: You can buy or sell during market hours.

slides.closing: One buy, many holdings. That's an [[ETF]].

slides.headline: Why people like [[ETFs]].
slides.sub: They spread your money across many companies.

rows.text: Easy to **buy and sell** like a share

slides.note: Fees and holdings vary from one ETF to another.

slides.headline: Check before you [[buy]].
slides.sub: Not all ETFs are the same.
slides.note: Educational only. Not a recommendation of any fund.

slides.title: ETF = A basket
slides.sub: One purchase, many investments.
checks: Buy it **in one go**, like a share

posts.caption:
Diversification, explained simply 👇

Diversification means spreading your money across different investments, so one bad result doesn't sink everything. It reduces risk, but it can't remove it.

Save this for the next time someone throws finance jargon at you. 🔖

New term every day. Follow @equivisionbasics.

Educational content only, not financial advice.

#diversification #investing #finance #personalfinance #financialliteracy #moneybasics #learnfinance

slides.headline: Diversification means [[not putting all your eggs]] in one basket.
slides.footer: Spread your money to spread your [[risk]].

slides.label: SAME DROP, LESS PAIN
slides.headline: Spread it out.
slides.sub: One company falls 50%. See the difference.

chart.title: Money lost when one company falls 50%

slides.note: Illustrative example. Diversifying reduces risk but doesn't remove it.

slides.headline: A [[smoother]] ride.
slides.sub: Different investments rise and fall at different times.

rows.text: It **doesn't remove** risk or guarantee profit

slides.note: The idea applies to stocks, bonds, funds and more.

slides.title: Diversify = Spread
slides.sub: Different baskets, smaller shocks.
checks: Don't put **all your money** in one place
Spreading out **shrinks the damage** of one loss
It **reduces** risk but can't remove it

posts.caption:
Compounding, explained simply 👇

Compounding means earning interest on your interest too, so growth builds on growth. Think of a snowball that gets bigger the longer it rolls.

Save this for the next time someone throws finance jargon at you. 🔖

New term every day. Follow @equivisionbasics.

Educational content only, not financial advice.

#compoundinterest #compounding #finance #personalfinance #financialliteracy #moneybasics #learnfinance

slides.headline: Compounding is earning [[interest]] on your interest too.
slides.footer: Think snowball: it grows [[faster as it rolls]].

slides.headline: You save [[$100]] at 10% interest a year.

slides.label: TIME IS THE SECRET
slides.headline: Same money, more time.
slides.sub: Compounding gets [[stronger the longer]] you wait.
slides.note: Assumes a steady 10% a year, which is high. Real returns vary.

slides.headline: It works for you, and [[against]] you.
slides.sub: The same effect applies to savings and to debt.

rows.text: Debt compounds too: **interest on interest** works against you

slides.note: Example numbers are for illustration only.

slides.title: Compounding = Snowball
slides.sub: Interest that earns interest.

posts.caption:
Bond, explained simply 👇

A bond is a loan you give to a company or a government. In return they pay you interest and give your money back on a set date.

Save this for the next time someone throws finance jargon at you. 🔖

New term every day. Follow @equivisionbasics.

Educational content only, not financial advice.

#bonds #investing #finance #personalfinance #financialliteracy #moneybasics #learnfinance

slides.headline: A bond is a [[loan]] you give to a company or government.
You lend a government [[$1,000]] for 5 years.

steps.title: It pays interest, say 4% a year
At the end, you get $1,000 back

slides.closing: A loan with a schedule. That's a [[bond]].

slides.label: BOND VS STOCK
slides.headline: Lender or [[owner]]?
slides.sub: The two behave very differently.

rows.text: You **lent** money. Payments are **set in advance**.

slides.note: Terms differ from bond to bond.

slides.headline: Bonds have [[risks]] too.
slides.sub: They're often steadier than stocks, but not risk-free.

rows.text: When rates rise, existing bonds **lose value**

slides.title: Bond = A loan
slides.sub: You lend. They repay with interest.
